definition: Parasitic means living on or in a host organism and benefiting at that host's expense.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word parasitic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know parasitic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The parasitic mistletoe taps the oak's own sap channels and gives the tree nothing in return.
Dependent says only that one organism needs another, while parasitic adds that the host pays the cost of that need.
Ruinous is stronger than parasitic, since many parasites weaken a host that survives for years, while a ruinous infestation destroys it outright.

Leeching is the vivid, accusing word for draining a person or system a little at a time, the way a leech draws blood. Parasitic is the biologist's term for the whole arrangement: one organism living on or in a host and profiting at that host's cost.

In ancient Greece a parasitos was a 'beside-eater' — a flatterer who turned up at a rich man's table to eat his sitos, his grain. That food-root built no other common English word, so it survives only in parasite itself. Keep the dinner-table picture: a parasitic thing feeds at someone else's expense while giving nothing back.
Parasitic means living on or in a host organism and benefiting at that host's expense.
A cuckoo lays one egg in a reed warbler's nest and flies away.
The warbler incubates it, and the cuckoo chick, larger and quicker to hatch, pushes the warbler's own eggs over the rim.
For six weeks the pair of warblers hunt insects from dawn to dusk to feed a chick three times their size, and raise none of their own young.
The cuckoo's parasitic strategy costs its host an entire breeding season.
The cuckoo gains a whole season of free care while the warblers lose every one of their own young, and benefit to one at the direct expense of the host is what parasitic means.
scientific; also figurative and insulting

In biology a parasite takes from a living host over time and usually does not kill it outright, which separates parasitic from predatory in this unit: a predator kills and eats its prey, while a parasite feeds on a host kept alive to go on feeding it.

The common cuckoo never builds a nest, never incubates an egg, and never feeds a chick.
Instead the female watches a pair of reed warblers build, slips in while they are away, and lays a single egg that closely matches theirs.
The relationship is purely parasitic: the warblers pay the whole cost of raising her chick, and they pay in more than food.
Within hours of hatching, the young cuckoo heaves the warblers' own eggs over the rim of the nest, one by one.
For weeks afterwards the pair works from dawn to dusk to fill a mouth wider than their own heads, feeding a stranger while their own brood lies in the grass below.
